commit_message:
grep -F: fix a heap buffer (read) overrun

grep's read buffer is often filled to its full size, except when
reading the final buffer of a file.  In that case, the number of
bytes read may be far less than the size of the buffer.  However, for
certain unusual pattern/text combinations, grep -F would mistakenly
examine bytes in that uninitialized region of memory when searching
for a match.  With carefully chosen inputs, one can cause grep -F to
read beyond the end of that buffer altogether.  This problem arose via
commit v2.18-90-g73893ff with the introduction of a more efficient
heuristic using what is now the memchr_kwset function. The use of
that function in bmexec_trans could leave TP much larger than EP,
and the subsequent call to bm_delta2_search would mistakenly access
beyond end of the main input read buffer.

* src/kwset.c (bmexec_trans): When TP reaches or exceeds EP,
do not call bm_delta2_search.
* tests/kwset-abuse: New file.
* tests/Makefile.am (TESTS): Add it.
* THANKS.in: Update.
* NEWS (Bug fixes): Mention it.

Prior to this patch, this command would trigger a UMR:

  printf %0360db 0 | valgrind src/grep -F $(printf %019dXb 0)

  Use of uninitialised value of size 8
     at 0x4142BE: bmexec_trans (kwset.c:657)
     by 0x4143CA: bmexec (kwset.c:678)
     by 0x414973: kwsexec (kwset.c:848)
     by 0x414DC4: Fexecute (kwsearch.c:128)
     by 0x404E2E: grepbuf (grep.c:1238)
     by 0x4054BF: grep (grep.c:1417)
     by 0x405CEB: grepdesc (grep.c:1645)
     by 0x405EC1: grep_command_line_arg (grep.c:1692)
     by 0x4077D4: main (grep.c:2570)

See the accompanying test for how to trigger the heap buffer overrun.

Thanks to Nima Aghdaii for testing and finding numerous
ways to break early iterations of this patch.
cve_desc: The bmexec_trans function in kwset.c in grep 2.19 through 2.21 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap read and crash) via crafted input when using the -F option.

commit_message:
bpf, ringbuf: Deny reserve of buffers larger than ringbuf

A BPF program might try to reserve a buffer larger than the ringbuf size.
If the consumer pointer is way ahead of the producer, that would be
successfully reserved, allowing the BPF program to read or write out of
the ringbuf allocated area.

Reported-by: Ryota Shiga (Flatt Security)
Fixes: 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it")
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
cve_desc: The eBPF RINGBUF bpf_ringbuf_reserve() function in the Linux kernel did not check that the allocated size was smaller than the ringbuf size, allowing an attacker to perform out-of-bounds writes within the kernel and therefore, arbitrary code execution. This issue was fixed via commit 4b81ccebaeee ("bpf, ringbuf: Deny reserve of buffers larger than ringbuf") (v5.13-rc4) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. It was introduced via 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it") (v5.8-rc1).

commit_message:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions during TensorFlow's Grappler optimizer phase, constant folding might attempt to deep copy a resource tensor. This results in a segfault, as these tensors are supposed to not change. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
Fixed Array.prototype.slice() with slow "this" argument.

Previously, when "this" argument was not a fast array, but the "deleted" array
was a fast array, the "deleted" array may be left in uninitialized state if
"this" argument had gaps.

This fix is to ensure that "deleted" is properly initialized.

This fixes #485 issue on Github.

sungem: switch to use qemu_receive_packet() for loopback

This patch switches to use qemu_receive_packet() which can detect
reentrancy and return early.

This is intended to address CVE-2021-3416.

Cc: Prasad J Pandit <ppandit@redhat.com>
Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Reviewed-by: Mark Cave-Ayland <mark.cave-ayland@ilande.co.uk>

Reviewed-by: Alistair Francis <alistair.francis@wdc.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
cve_desc: A potential stack overflow via infinite loop issue was found in various NIC emulators of QEMU in versions up to and including 5.2.0. The issue occurs in loopback mode of a NIC wherein reentrant DMA checks get bypassed. A guest user/process may use this flaw to consume CPU cycles or crash the QEMU process on the host resulting in DoS scenario.

fix(plugin): Add default limits for chunks and message size

Based on a reported DoS vulnerability reported by Team82 (Claroty
Research).
cve_desc: The package open62541/open62541 before 1.2.5, from 1.3-rc1 and before 1.3.1 are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) due to a missing limitation on the number of received chunks - per single session or in total for all concurrent sessions. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending an unlimited number of huge chunks (e.g. 2GB each) without sending the Final closing chunk.

commit_message:
PCI: rpadlpar: Fix potential drc_name corruption in store functions

Both add_slot_store() and remove_slot_store() try to fix up the
drc_name copied from the store buffer by placing a NUL terminator at
nbyte + 1 or in place of a '\n' if present. However, the static buffer
that we copy the drc_name data into is not zeroed and can contain
anything past the n-th byte.

This is problematic if a '\n' byte appears in that buffer after nbytes
and the string copied into the store buffer was not NUL terminated to
start with as the strchr() search for a '\n' byte will mark this
incorrectly as the end of the drc_name string resulting in a drc_name
string that contains garbage data after the n-th byte.

Additionally it will cause us to overwrite that '\n' byte on the stack
with NUL, potentially corrupting data on the stack.

The following debugging shows an example of the drmgr utility writing
"PHB 4543" to the add_slot sysfs attribute, but add_slot_store()
logging a corrupted string value.

  drmgr: drmgr: -c phb -a -s PHB 4543 -d 1
  add_slot_store: drc_name = PHB 4543°|<82>!, rc = -19

Fix this by using strscpy() instead of memcpy() to ensure the string
is NUL terminated when copied into the static drc_name buffer.
Further, since the string is now NUL terminated the code only needs to
change '\n' to '\0' when present.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Tyrel Datwyler <tyreld@linux.ibm.com>
[mpe: Reformat change log and add mention of possible stack corruption]
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210315214821.452959-1-tyreld@linux.ibm.com
cve_desc: In drivers/pci/hotplug/rpadlpar_sysfs.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8, the RPA PCI Hotplug driver has a user-tolerable buffer overflow when writing a new device name to the driver from userspace, allowing userspace to write data to the kernel stack frame directly. This occurs because add_slot_store and remove_slot_store mishandle drc_name '\0' termination, aka CID-cc7a0bb058b8.

cve_desc: ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP before 5.6.25 and 7.x before 7.0.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via an invalid wddxPacket XML document that is mishandled in a wddx_deserialize call, as demonstrated by a stray element inside a boolean element, leading to incorrect pop processing.
reasoning:
<think>
Okay, let's tackle this. I need to analyze the provided C code from PHP's WDDX handling to identify any security vulnerabilities. The user wants a JSON output indicating if a vulnerability was detected, the vulnerabilities found, and the reasoning with confidence.

First, I'll go through the code step by step. The function php_wddx_pop_element is part of the WDDX parser, which deals with deserializing data. The main points to check are how it handles objects, especially during deserialization, since that's a common source of vulnerabilities.

Looking at the code, there's a section where it checks if the data type is IS_OBJECT. When that's the case, it calls the __wakeup() method using call_user_function_ex. The __wakeup() method is similar to a constructor and is called during deserialization. If an attacker can control the object being deserialized, they might inject an object that triggers __wakeup() with malicious code. This is a known issue in PHP deserialization vulnerabilities. So that's a potential problem.

Another part is where it handles the class name. When the varname is PHP_CLASS_NAME_VAR, it takes the string value from ent1->data, converts it to lowercase, and uses it to find a class entry in the class table. If the class isn't found, it uses PHP_IC_ENTRY (which might be a placeholder for incomplete classes). This could allow an attacker to specify any class name, leading to object injection if the class has vulnerable magic methods. The code doesn't seem to validate or sanitize the class name here, which is risky.

The code also uses functions like php_base64_decode for binary data, which is okay, but if the input is not validated, it could lead to issues, though that's less likely. The memory management with efree and zval_ptr_dtor seems proper, but if there's a use-after-free or double-free, that could be a problem. However, the code checks stack->top before accessing elements, which might mitigate some of that.

The author's explanation mentions that the __wakeup() call is a risk, and the class name resolution could allow arbitrary class instantiation. The absence of input validation here is a vulnerability. The code doesn't check if the class name is safe or if the data comes from a trusted source. Since WDDX can be used to exchange data, if an attacker can control the input, they could exploit these issues.

So, the vulnerabilities here are:

1. Deserialization of objects leading to __wakeup() call without input validation, allowing potential code execution or other attacks.
2. Unvalidated class name resolution when instantiating objects, which could lead to object injection.

The confidence is high because these are well-known issues in deserialization, and the code directly calls __wakeup() and uses user-controlled data for class names without checks. The absence of validation or sanitization here is a clear vulnerability.

commit_message:
Cleanup and remove duplicate validation in `SparseCount`.

We have valdiation that is duplicated, checking different conditions, in different formats and failing to capture all cases. This should fix all the previous bugs.

cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `SparseCountSparseOutput` is vulnerable to a heap overflow. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
bpf: Fix integer overflow in prealloc_elems_and_freelist()

In prealloc_elems_and_freelist(), the multiplication to calculate the
size passed to bpf_map_area_alloc() could lead to an integer overflow.
As a result, out-of-bounds write could occur in pcpu_freelist_populate()
as reported by KASAN:

[...]
[   16.968613] BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in pcpu_freelist_populate+0xd9/0x100
[   16.969408] Write of size 8 at addr ffff888104fc6ea0 by task crash/78
[   16.970038]
[   16.970195] CPU: 0 PID: 78 Comm: crash Not tainted 5.15.0-rc2+ #1
[   16.970878] Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS 1.13.0-1ubuntu1.1 04/01/2014
[   16.972026] Call Trace:
[   16.972306]  dump_stack_lvl+0x34/0x44
[   16.972687]  print_address_description.constprop.0+0x21/0x140
[   16.973297]  ? pcpu_freelist_populate+0xd9/0x100
[   16.973777]  ? pcpu_freelist_populate+0xd9/0x100
[   16.974257]  kasan_report.cold+0x7f/0x11b
[   16.974681]  ? pcpu_freelist_populate+0xd9/0x100
[   16.975190]  pcpu_freelist_populate+0xd9/0x100
[   16.975669]  stack_map_alloc+0x209/0x2a0
[   16.976106]  __sys_bpf+0xd83/0x2ce0
[...]

The possibility of this overflow was originally discussed in [0], but
was overlooked.

Fix the integer overflow by changing elem_size to u64 from u32.

  [0] https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/728b238e-a481-eb50-98e9-b0f430ab01e7@gmail.com/

Fixes: 557c0c6e7df8 ("bpf: convert stackmap to pre-allocation")
Signed-off-by: Tatsuhiko Yasumatsu <th.yasumatsu@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/20210930135545.173698-1-th.yasumatsu@gmail.com
cve_desc: prealloc_elems_and_freelist in kernel/bpf/stackmap.c in the Linux kernel before 5.14.12 allows unprivileged users to trigger an eBPF multiplication integer overflow with a resultant out-of-bounds write.

commit_message:
rsi: fix a double free bug in rsi_91x_deinit()

`dev` (struct rsi_91x_usbdev *) field of adapter
(struct rsi_91x_usbdev *) is allocated  and initialized in
`rsi_init_usb_interface`. If any error is detected in information
read from the device side,  `rsi_init_usb_interface` will be
freed. However, in the higher level error handling code in
`rsi_probe`, if error is detected, `rsi_91x_deinit` is called
again, in which `dev` will be freed again, resulting double free.

This patch fixes the double free by removing the free operation on
`dev` in `rsi_init_usb_interface`, because `rsi_91x_deinit` is also
used in `rsi_disconnect`, in that code path, the `dev` field is not
 (and thus needs to be) freed.

This bug was found in v4.19, but is also present in the latest version
of kernel. Fixes CVE-2019-15504.

Reported-by: Hui Peng <benquike@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Mathias Payer <mathias.payer@nebelwelt.net>
Signed-off-by: Hui Peng <benquike@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Guenter Roeck <linux@roeck-us.net>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
cve_desc: drivers/net/wireless/rsi/rsi_91x_usb.c in the Linux kernel through 5.2.9 has a Double Free via crafted USB device traffic (which may be remote via usbip or usbredir).

Another possible issue: the tx_buffer is allocated with kmalloc(2048, GFP_KERNEL). If the hardware requires a specific buffer size or alignment, using a fixed size might be problematic. But unless there's a specific reason, this might not be a vulnerability, but the user mentioned that absence of security measures is a vulnerability. First, the function starts by allocating memory for rsi_dev using kzalloc. If that fails, it returns -ENOMEM. That's standard error handling. Then it assigns the adapter's rsi_dev pointer to this new memory. The USB device is obtained from the pfunction interface using interface_to_usbdev, and the priv field is set to the adapter. So far, so good.

Next, there's a call to rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints. If that returns an error, the status is set to -EINVAL and it jumps to fail_eps. That makes sense because if the endpoints aren't found, the interface can't be properly initialized. The error code here is EINVAL, which is appropriate for invalid arguments or configurations.

Then, the device is set to the pfunction's dev, and usb_set_intfdata is called to associate the adapter with the interface. That's standard practice for USB drivers to store their private data.

The code then allocates a tx_buffer of 2048 bytes. If that fails, it goes to fail_eps. The buffer size is fixed at 2048, which might be a design choice based on the device's requirements. But why 2048? Maybe that's the maximum packet size the device can handle, or a multiple of some block size. The tx_blk_size is set to 252, which is a bit odd. Wait, 2048 divided by 252 is about 8.13, so maybe each block is 252 bytes, and the buffer can hold 8 blocks? Or maybe there's some overhead. That could be a potential issue if the buffer size isn't a multiple of the block size, leading to inefficiencies or possible buffer overflows if not handled correctly.

Then there's a call to rsi_usb_init_rx, which initializes the receive handle. If that fails, it logs an error and jumps to fail_rx, which frees the tx_buffer before going to fail_eps. The error handling here seems okay, but the order of cleanup could be important. For example, if rsi_usb_init_rx allocates other resources, they should be freed here, but the code only frees tx_buffer. If rsi_usb_init_rx fails after allocating other resources, those might leak. But maybe that function handles its own cleanup on failure.

The function then sets up some function callbacks for the adapter, like check_hw_queue_status and determine_event_timeout, which are specific to USB. The host interface is set to USB, and the host_intf_ops is assigned to usb_host_intf_ops. That makes sense for differentiating between different host interfaces (like USB vs. SDIO).

There's a debugfs part under a config option, which reduces the number of debugfs entries by one. Not sure why, but maybe the USB implementation has a different requirement or a known issue that requires one less entry.

The function ends with a debug message indicating success.

Potential risky parts: The fixed buffer size of 2048 and block size of 252. If the device requires a different buffer size or if the block size isn't correctly calculated, it could lead to issues. Also, error handling in rsi_usb_init_rx might not clean up all allocated resources if it fails. Another thing is that the code uses GFP_KERNEL for allocations, which can sleep, but if this function is called in a context that can't sleep (like interrupt context), that could be a problem. However, since it's a USB interface init, it's likely called during device probing, which is in a process context, so that's probably okay.

Another point is that the error handling jumps to fail_eps after fail_rx, which frees the tx_buffer. But if other resources were allocated before that, like in rsi_usb_init_rx, they might not be freed. For example, if rsi_usb_init_rx allocates some DMA buffers or other structures, those would need to be freed in the fail_rx path. If not, that's a memory leak.

Also, the function doesn't check if the USB device (rsi_dev->usbdev) is valid after assignment. If interface_to_usbdev could return NULL, that should be checked. But in the context of a USB driver's probe function, the pfunction should be valid, so maybe that's not a concern here.

In terms of design choices, using fixed buffer sizes might be based on the specific hardware requirements. The separation of USB-specific operations into callbacks (like check_hw_queue_status) allows for different host interfaces (like SDIO) to have their own implementations, which is good for code modularity.

So, the main potential issues are possible resource leaks in error paths and the fixed buffer/block sizes which might not be flexible or could lead to inefficiencies or overflows if not properly managed.

commit_message:
Remove a `DCHECK`-fail, log an error instead.

`DCHECK` in debug mode results in crashes. TensorFlow has had multiple vulnerabilities due to this.

Outside of debug mode, `DCHECK` is a no-op.

A better alternative is to report an error to the log buffer and continue. This should happen both in debug mode and in prod mode.

commit_message:
Fix a bug when getting a gzip header extra field with inflate().

If the extra field was larger than the space the user provided with
inflateGetHeader(), and if multiple calls of inflate() delivered
the extra header data, then there could be a buffer overflow of the
provided space. This commit assures that provided space is not
exceeded.
cve_desc: zlib through 1.2.12 has a heap-based buffer over-read or buffer overflow in inflate in inflate.c via a large gzip header extra field. NOTE: only applications that call inflateGetHeader are affected. Some common applications bundle the affected zlib source code but may be unable to call inflateGetHeader (e.g., see the nodejs/node reference).

commit_message:
Prevent nullptr deref in SparseTensorSliceDataset

The arguments must determine a valid sparse tensor. This means that when indices are empty then the values must be empty too (and the reverse).

Also added test, by modifying existing test with empty sparse tensor to now run with an invalid sparse tensor input.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 388562757
Change-Id: Id8b54cd7c2316025b4f9a77292c8fb5344d17609
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. When a user does not supply arguments that determine a valid sparse tensor, `tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorSliceDataset` implementation can be made to dereference a null pointer. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/data/sparse_tensor_slice_dataset_op.cc#L240-L251) has some argument validation but fails to consider the case when either `indices` or `values` are provided for an empty sparse tensor when the other is not. If `indices` is empty, then [code that performs validation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/data/sparse_tensor_slice_dataset_op.cc#L260-L261) (i.e., checking that the indices are monotonically increasing) results in a null pointer dereference. If `indices` as provided by the user is empty, then `indices` in the C++ code above is backed by an empty `std::vector`, hence calling `indices->dim_size(0)` results in null pointer dereferencing (same as calling `std::vector::at()` on an empty vector). We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 02cc160e29d20631de3859c6653184e3f876b9d7. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message: Fix oob write for dwarf with abbrev with count 0 (Fix #2083) (#2086)
cve_desc: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. In versions up to and including 0.3.1 there is a heap-based out of bounds write in parse_die() when reversing an AMD64 ELF binary with DWARF debug info. When a malicious AMD64 ELF binary is opened by a victim user, Rizin may crash or execute unintended actions. No workaround are known and users are advised to upgrade.

The loop runs from i=0 to abbrev->count -1. Wait, the loop condition is i < abbrev->count -1. That seems off. If abbrev->count is the number of attributes, then the loop should go up to i < abbrev->count, right? Because if count is 5, the indices are 0-4, so the loop would run 5 times. But here, it's i < count -1, which would run 4 times for count=5. That's an off-by-one error. This means the last attribute isn't processed, leading to incomplete data. messages. Add checks like for other types of vhost-user messages.

Fixes: d87f1a1cb7b6 ("vhost: support inflight info sharing")
Cc: stable@dpdk.org

Signed-off-by: David Marchand <david.marchand@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Maxime Coquelin <maxime.coquelin@redhat.com>

This flaw allows a malicious vhost-user master to attach an unexpected number of fds as ancillary data to VHOST_USER_GET_INFLIGHT_FD / VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD messages that are not closed by the vhost-user slave. By sending such messages continuously, the vhost-user master exhausts available fd in the vhost-user slave process, leading to a denial of service.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation for `tf.raw_ops.FractionalAvgPoolGrad` can be tricked into accessing data outside of bounds of heap allocated buffers. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/f24faa153ad31a4b51578f8181d3aaab77a1ddeb/tensorflow/core/kernels/fractional_avg_pool_op.cc#L205) does not validate that the input tensor is non-empty. Thus, code constructs an empty `EigenDoubleMatrixMap` and then accesses this buffer with indices that are outside of the empty area. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 0f931751fb20f565c4e94aa6df58d54a003cdb30. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

rsi: release skb if rsi_prepare_beacon fails

In rsi_send_beacon, if rsi_prepare_beacon fails the allocated skb should
be released.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
cve_desc: A memory leak in the rsi_send_beacon() function in drivers/net/wireless/rsi/rsi_91x_mgmt.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering rsi_prepare_beacon() failures, aka CID-d563131ef23c.
reasoning:

Okay, let's tackle this. The user wants me to act as a Security Analyst and determine if the provided code has vulnerabilities. The code is a function called rsi_send_beacon in a wireless driver. The author's explanation points out some issues, but I need to verify and structure the response properly.

First, I'll look at the code step by step. The function starts by allocating a socket buffer (sk_buff) with dev_alloc_skb. If allocation fails, it returns -ENOMEM. Then it initializes the skb data to zero. Next, there's a part where they calculate dword_align_bytes by masking the data pointer with 0x3f (which is 63 in decimal). This is to check the alignment. If the data isn't aligned, they use skb_pull to adjust it. 

Wait, the problem here is that skb_pull moves the data pointer backward. If the original data pointer isn't aligned, subtracting (64 - align_bytes) could make the data pointer point before the start of the allocated buffer. For example, if the data starts at address 0x1000 + 10, align_bytes is 10. 64 - 10 is 54. So skb_pull(skb, 54) would set data to 0x1000 +10 -54 = 0x1000 -44. But the buffer was allocated starting at 0x1000, so accessing data before that is invalid. This leads to memory corruption or crashes.

Another issue is the memset. The code does memset(skb->data, 0, MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) before adjusting the data pointer. If the data pointer is moved backward, the memset didn't cover the new area. So the actual data used after alignment might not be initialized, leading to possible data corruption or information leakage.

The author's explanation mentions these points. So the vulnerabilities here are incorrect buffer alignment handling leading to memory access violations and improper initialization of the buffer after alignment.

commit_message:
vnc: sanitize bits_per_pixel from the client

bits_per_pixel that are less than 8 could result in accessing
non-initialized buffers later in the code due to the expectation
that bytes_per_pixel value that is used to initialize these buffers is
never zero.

To fix this check that bits_per_pixel from the client is one of the
values that the rfb protocol specification allows.

This is CVE-2014-7815.

Signed-off-by: Petr Matousek <pmatouse@redhat.com>

[ kraxel: apply codestyle fix ]

Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>

cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementations of `Sparse*Cwise*` ops are vulnerable to integer overflows. These can be used to trigger large allocations (so, OOM based denial of service) or `CHECK`-fails when building new `TensorShape` objects (so, assert failures based denial of service). We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
parallels: Sanity check for s->tracks (CVE-2014-0142)

This avoids a possible division by zero.

Convert s->tracks to unsigned as well because it feels better than
surviving just because the results of calculations with s->tracks are
converted to unsigned anyway.

Signed-off-by: Kevin Wolf <kwolf@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Max Reitz <mreitz@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
cve_desc: QEMU, possibly before 2.0.0, allows local users to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and crash) via a zero value in the (1) tracks field to the seek_to_sector function in block/parallels.c or (2) extent_size field in the bochs function in block/bochs.c.

First, the code sets the block device to read-only. That's a design choice, but the comment says "no write support yet," which might indicate that future write support could introduce vulnerabilities, but for now, it's not an issue.

Next, it reads the header and checks the magic and version. That's standard for format validation. The use of le32_to_cpu suggests proper handling of endianness, which is good.

Then, it checks if tracks are zero, which is a valid check. The catalog_size is checked against INT_MAX / 4 to prevent integer overflow during allocation. That's a good practice. However, after allocating memory with g_malloc for s->catalog_bitmap, there's no check if the allocation failed. If g_malloc returns NULL, the subsequent bdrv_pread would write to a NULL pointer, leading to a crash or potential exploit. This is a critical issue because memory allocation can fail under certain conditions, like low memory, and not handling it is a vulnerability.

The code also uses a mutex for locking, which is appropriate for thread safety in QEMU's environment. The error handling uses a fail label to clean up, which is good, but the missing check for allocation failure is a problem.

So, the main vulnerability here is the missing check for the allocation failure of s->catalog_bitmap. Even though the code checks other conditions, this oversight could lead to a null pointer dereference, which is a security risk.
</think>

  "vulnerabilities": [
    {
      "type": "Memory Allocation Failure Handling",
      "description": "Missing check for g_malloc failure in s->catalog_bitmap allocation"

  "analysis": "The code allocates memory for s->catalog_bitmap using g_malloc but does not verify if the allocation succeeded. }

commit_message:
ax25: Fix UAF bugs in ax25 timers

There are race conditions that may lead to UAF bugs in
ax25_heartbeat_expiry(), ax25_t1timer_expiry(), ax25_t2timer_expiry(),
ax25_t3timer_expiry() and ax25_idletimer_expiry(), when we call
ax25_release() to deallocate ax25_dev.

One of the UAF bugs caused by ax25_release() is shown below:

      (Thread 1)                    |      (Thread 2)
ax25_dev_device_up() //(1)          |
...                                 | ax25_kill_by_device()
ax25_bind()          //(2)          |
ax25_connect()                      | ...
 ax25_std_establish_data_link()     |
  ax25_start_t1timer()              | ax25_dev_device_down() //(3)
   mod_timer(&ax25->t1timer,..)     |
                                    | ax25_release()
   (wait a time)                    |  ...
                                    |  ax25_dev_put(ax25_dev) //(4)FREE
   ax25_t1timer_expiry()            |
    ax25->ax25_dev->values[..] //USE|  ...
     ...                            |

We increase the refcount of ax25_dev in position (1) and (2), and
decrease the refcount of ax25_dev in position (3) and (4).
The ax25_dev will be freed in position (4) and be used in
ax25_t1timer_expiry().

The fail log is shown below:
==============================================================

[  106.116942] BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in ax25_t1timer_expiry+0x1c/0x60
[  106.116942] Read of size 8 at addr ffff88800bda9028 by task swapper/0/0
[  106.116942] CPU: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 5.17.0-06123-g0905eec574
[  106.116942] Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS rel-14
[  106.116942] Call Trace:
...
[  106.116942]  ax25_t1timer_expiry+0x1c/0x60
[  106.116942]  call_timer_fn+0x122/0x3d0
[  106.116942]  __run_timers.part.0+0x3f6/0x520
[  106.116942]  run_timer_softirq+0x4f/0xb0
[  106.116942]  __do_softirq+0x1c2/0x651
...

This patch adds del_timer_sync() in ax25_release(), which could ensure
that all timers stop before we deallocate ax25_dev.

Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
cve_desc: A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s Amateur Radio AX.25 protocol functionality in the way a user connects with the protocol. This flaw allows a local user to crash the system.

However, the code uses lock_sock and release_sock, which should serialize access. But maybe there's a window where the lock is released and the state is inconsistent. Next, timers. The code calls del_timer_sync on several timers. The del_timer_sync function ensures that the timer is stopped before proceeding. However, if the timer callback is still running in another CPU, there could be a race. But del_timer_sync should handle that by waiting for the callback to finish. For example, after ax25_destroy_socket is called, which presumably frees the ax25 structure, but if a timer is still pending and its callback uses that structure, it would be a use-after-free. But before that, they check if sk is not NULL, but do they stop the timers? Let me check the code again.

Looking at the code structure: after the big if (sk->sk_type == SOCK_SEQPACKET) block, there's a section that runs regardless of socket type. In that section, they check if ax25_dev exists and then delete all timers (del_timer_sync on timer, t1, t2, t3, idletimer). Then they put the device. So in all cases, the timers are deleted. But ax25_destroy_socket is called in some paths before this. For example, in the case of state 0, they call ax25_destroy_socket inside the case. Then, after the switch, they proceed to delete the timers. Wait, no. Let me check the code flow.

In the case of SOCK_SEQPACKET:

- For state 0: they call ax25_destroy_socket inside the case, then break. Then after the switch, they check if ax25_dev exists and delete timers, etc.

Wait, no. The code structure is:

if (sk->sk_type == SOCK_SEQPACKET) {
    switch (ax25->state) {
        case 0:
            ... 
            ax25_destroy_socket(ax25);
            break;
        case 1/2:
            ...
            if (!sock_flag(...))
                ax25_destroy_socket(ax25);
            break;
        case 3/4:
            ... 
            break;
    }
} else {
    ... 
    ax25_destroy_socket(ax25);
}

Then, after the if/else block, the code checks if ax25_dev exists and deletes all timers, then does dev_put, etc.

So in the case of state 0, ax25_destroy_socket is called inside the case, then after the switch, the code proceeds to delete the timers. But if ax25_destroy_socket frees the ax25 structure, then accessing ax25_dev (which is part of the ax25 structure) after that would be a use-after-free. Because after ax25_destroy_socket is called, the ax25 pointer may no longer be valid. But in the code, after the switch, they check if ax25_dev exists (ax25_dev = ax25->ax25_dev; earlier, but ax25 could have been freed by ax25_destroy_socket). Wait, let's see:

In the code:

ax25 = sk_to_ax25(sk);
ax25_dev = ax25->ax25_dev;

These are obtained before the switch. So even if ax25_destroy_socket is called inside the case (like in state 0), the ax25 and ax25_dev variables here are still pointing to the same memory, but the structure may have been freed. So when the code proceeds to check if ax25_dev exists and then calls del_timer_sync on the timers (which are part of the ax25 structure), that would be accessing freed memory. That's a use-after-free vulnerability.

For example, in the case of state 0:

They call ax25_destroy_socket(ax25), which presumably frees the ax25 structure. Then, after the switch, the code checks if ax25_dev (which was ax25->ax25_dev before the destroy) exists. But since ax25 has been freed, accessing ax25_dev is invalid. Then, they call del_timer_sync on timers that were part of the ax25 structure, which is now freed. This is a clear use-after-free.

This is a critical vulnerability. The code destroys the socket (ax25_destroy_socket) but then continues to access the ax25 structure's members (like ax25_dev and the timers) after it's been freed. That's a definite issue.

Another point: in the case of state 1/2, they check if the socket is not destroyed before calling ax25_destroy_socket. But if the socket is destroyed, they don't call it. However, after that, the code still proceeds to delete the timers and access ax25_dev. But if ax25_destroy_socket was not called, then the ax25 structure is still valid. But in the case where ax25_destroy_socket was called (like in state 0), then the structure is freed, leading to UaF.

So the main vulnerability here is use-after-free in the code paths where ax25_destroy_socket is called before the final cleanup section. The code assumes that the ax25 structure is still valid after calling ax25_destroy_socket, which is incorrect.

Another possible issue is the locking. The code calls lock_sock(sk) and release_sock(sk) in various places. For example, in state 0, they release the sock lock, then relock it. But during the time the lock is released, another thread could access the socket and see an inconsistent state. However, since the socket is being released, perhaps it's okay. But I'm not sure. The main issue seems to be the use-after-free.

So the vulnerabilities detected are:

1. Use-after-free when accessing ax25 structure members after ax25_destroy_socket is called in certain code paths.

2. Possible race conditions in state transitions if the locking is not sufficient, but the code uses lock_sock which should protect the socket structure.

The first one is a definite vulnerability. The second is possible but less certain.

So the JSON should reflect that vulnerability_detected is true, with the use-after-free as the main issue.
</think>

commit_message:
Fix a null pointer exception in SVDF

This is due to not checking that `GetVariableInput` returns non-null tensor.

Also fix a potential null pointer exception in `GetVariableInput`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385160147
Change-Id: Iadf3f0705b036a9014d27caa5a8bbd91f4c4c401
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of SVDF in TFLite is [vulnerable to a null pointer error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/svdf.cc#L300-L313). The [`GetVariableInput` function](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L115-L119) can return a null pointer but `GetTensorData` assumes that the argument is always a valid tensor. Furthermore, because `GetVariableInput` calls [`GetMutableInput`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L82-L90) which might return `nullptr`, the `tensor->is_variable` expression can also trigger a null pointer exception. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 5b048e87e4e55990dae6b547add4dae59f4e1c76. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
ip6_gre: fix ip6gre_err() invalid reads

Andrey Konovalov reported out of bound accesses in ip6gre_err()

If GRE flags contains GRE_KEY, the following expression
*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1)

accesses data ~40 bytes after the expected point, since
grehlen includes the size of IPv6 headers.

Let's use a "struct gre_base_hdr *greh" pointer to make this
code more readable.

p[1] becomes greh->protocol.
grhlen is the GRE header length.

Fixes: c12b395a4664 ("gre: Support GRE over IPv6")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
cve_desc: The ip6gre_err function in net/ipv6/ip6_gre.c in the Linux kernel allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors involving GRE flags in an IPv6 packet, which trigger an out-of-bounds access.

Looking for potential vulnerabilities. The user mentioned that even minor issues should be flagged, and absence of security measures is a vulnerability. Let's check for common issues like buffer overflows, race conditions, improper input validation, etc.

Starting with the key_off calculation. The code checks if the GRE flags have GRE_KEY set, then calculates key_off as grehlen + offset. Then later, it accesses skb->data + key_off. But does it validate that key_off is within the packet's data length? The code uses pskb_may_pull for offset + grehlen, but when GRE_KEY is set, grehlen increases by 4. However, the second pskb_may_pull checks offset + grehlen again, which would include the key's 4 bytes. Wait, let me check:

The first check is pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen) after initial grehlen. Then, if GRE_KEY is set, grehlen increases by 4. Then there's another pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen). So that should cover the key's 4 bytes. So key_off is grehlen (original) + offset, but after the second pskb_may_pull, which checks offset + grehlen (now including the key's 4 bytes). Wait, no. Let me retrace:

Original grehlen is sizeof(greh), which is 8 bytes (assuming struct gre_base_hdr is 8 bytes). Then, if GRE_CSUM is set, grehlen +=4. If GRE_KEY is set, key_off is grehlen + offset, and grehlen +=4. Then, the second pskb_may_pull checks offset + grehlen. So the key is at offset + grehlen (original) + offset? Wait, no. Let me see:

The code:

flags = greh->flags;
if (flags & (GRE_VERSION | GRE_ROUTING))
    return;
if (flags & GRE_CSUM)
    grehlen += 4;
if (flags & GRE_KEY) {
    key_off = grehlen + offset;
    grehlen += 4;
}

Then, after that, there's another pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen). So the total grehlen after possible additions is checked. So the key is at key_off = grehlen (before adding 4 for key) + offset. Then grehlen is increased by 4. So the second pskb_may_pull checks offset + grehlen (which now includes the key's 4 bytes). Therefore, the key is within the checked data. So accessing skb->data + key_off should be safe because the second pskb_may_pull ensures that the entire GRE header including the key is present. So maybe that's not a vulnerability. Hmm, but maybe there's a miscalculation here. For example, if the initial grehlen is 8, then after adding 4 for GRE_CSUM, it's 12, then key_off is 12 + offset, then grehlen becomes 16. The second check is offset + 16. So the key is at offset + 12, which is within offset + 16. So that's okay. So maybe the key_off is safe. So perhaps the initial thought about out-of-bounds read is incorrect. But maybe there's a case where the offset is such that key_off exceeds the skb's data length. But the pskb_may_pull checks that the data is present up to offset + grehlen (which includes the key's 4 bytes). Therefore, the key_off is within the data. So maybe that's not a vulnerability.

Next, looking at the tunnel lookup. The code uses ip6gre_tunnel_lookup with the skb's dev, destination, source, key, and protocol. If the tunnel is found, it proceeds. This seems okay, as it's checking for a valid tunnel.

In the ICMPV6_PKT_TOOBIG case, the code sets the tunnel's MTU to mtu = be32_to_cpu(info) - offset. But info comes from the ICMP packet, which is untrusted. The code checks if mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU and sets it to that minimum. However, what if info is very small, leading to a negative mtu? For example, if info is 0, then mtu would be -offset. But offset is an int passed into the function. How is offset determined? The offset is passed as a parameter to ip6gre_err. If the offset is larger than info, then mtu could be negative. However, the code checks if mtu < IPV6_MIN_MTU (which is 1280), so if mtu is negative, it would set it to 1280. But is there a case where info could be so small that even after subtracting offset, it's negative? For example, if info is 100 and offset is 1000, then mtu would be -900. Then the code sets it to 1280. So that's safe. But maybe the code should validate that info is at least offset + some value. However, the code does check for that by setting a minimum. So maybe this is okay. But the user's instruction says to flag even minor issues. So perhaps the lack of validation on 'info' could be a problem. But the code does handle it by clamping to the minimum. So maybe not a vulnerability here.

Another point is the handling of the error counters (t->err_time and t->err_count). These are updated without any locking. If this function can be called from a softirq or concurrent context, there could be a race condition where multiple updates to err_count or err_time are lost. For example, if two ICMP errors arrive at the same time, the increments might not be atomic. In the kernel, accessing shared variables without proper synchronization can lead to race conditions. So this could be a vulnerability. The code uses time_before(jiffies, t->err_time + IP6TUNNEL_ERR_TIMEO) to check if the error is within a timeout, and increments err_count or resets it. If two calls to this function happen concurrently, the err_count might not be updated correctly. So this is a potential race condition.

Another thing: the code logs messages using net_dbg_ratelimited, which is rate-limited, so that's good to prevent log flooding. But the function itself doesn't have any rate limiting on the processing of ICMP errors, which could lead to high CPU usage if many errors are received. However, the kernel's networking stack typically handles this at a higher level, so maybe this is not a direct vulnerability here.

Looking at the tunnel lookup: the code uses the destination and source IPv6 addresses from the IPv6 header. If an attacker can spoof ICMPv6 packets with specific addresses, they might trick the system into updating an MTU for a tunnel they shouldn't. However, the tunnel lookup requires that the tunnel exists, so this would only affect existing tunnels. This is a common issue with ICMP handling, but the code doesn't have a specific vulnerability here beyond standard ICMP trust issues.

In the ICMPV6_PARAMPROB case, the code calls ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim(skb, skb->data), which parses a TLV (Type-Length-Value) from the packet. If this function doesn't properly validate the TLV's length, it could lead to out-of-bounds reads. However, the code checks if teli (the offset) equals be32_to_cpu(info) - 2. But without seeing the implementation of ip6_tnl_parse_tlv_enc_lim, it's hard to say. Assuming that function is safe, but if not, this could be a problem. However, since the user provided only this code, maybe we can't flag that unless there's an obvious issue here.

Putting it all together, the main potential vulnerabilities I can see are:

1. Race conditions in updating t->err_time and t->err_count without synchronization.
2. Possible issues with the MTU update from untrusted input, though the code clamps it to a minimum.
3. The key_off calculation might have an off-by-one or miscalculation, but the pskb_may_pull checks seem to cover it.

But according to the user's instruction, when in doubt, consider it vulnerable. So the race condition in error counters is a valid point. Also, the MTU update uses info from the ICMP packet without checking if info is at least offset + something. For example, if info is less than offset, then mtu would be negative, but the code sets it to IPV6_MIN_MTU. So that's handled. So maybe that's okay.

So the main vulnerability is the race condition in the error counters. Also, the code directly uses the key from the packet without validating that the tunnel actually uses a key. For example, if the tunnel is configured without a key, but the packet has a key, would that be a problem? The code looks up the tunnel using the key, so if the tunnel exists with that key, it's valid. But if the tunnel doesn't use keys, then the key would be zero, and the lookup would still find the tunnel. Hmm, but the tunnel lookup uses the key as part of the parameters. So if the tunnel is configured without a key, then the key in the packet would be ignored? Or does the lookup require the key to match? The code uses ip6gre_tunnel_lookup, which in the kernel typically matches based on the parameters including the key. So if the tunnel is configured with a key, then the key must match. If not, then any key would work. But this is part of the tunnel configuration, so it's up to the admin. Not a code vulnerability.

So the main issues are the race conditions in the error counters and possibly the MTU update. But the MTU is clamped, so maybe that's okay. The race condition is a real issue.

Another point: the code uses t->dev->mtu = mtu; directly. Changing the MTU of a device can have significant effects. If an attacker can send a crafted ICMPv6_PKT_TOOBIG packet, they could force the MTU to a very low value, causing fragmentation and potential denial of service. However, the code sets a minimum of IPV6_MIN_MTU (1280), so it can't be set lower than that. But 1280 is the standard minimum for IPv6, so that's acceptable. So this might not be a vulnerability.

So the main vulnerability is the race condition in the error counters. Also, the code doesn't check if the tunnel is valid after lookup. But the code checks if (!t) return; so that's okay.

Another thing: the function is called with parameters that come from the network (like type, code, info, offset). If these are not properly validated, they could be used to trigger issues. For example, the offset is used in several places. If the offset is very large, the pskb_may_pull checks would fail, and the function would return early. So that's handled.

So, in conclusion, the main vulnerability is the race condition in updating the error counters (t->err_time and t->err_count) without proper synchronization. This could lead to incorrect error counting or other concurrency issues.

Additionally, the code may have an issue with the key_off calculation. Wait, let me recheck. The key_off is set to grehlen + offset. Then grehlen is increased by 4. Then the second pskb_may_pull checks offset + grehlen (which is now grehlen_initial + 4 (if GRE_KEY is set) + offset). So the key is at offset + grehlen_initial, and the check is for offset + grehlen_initial + 4. So the key is within the checked data. Therefore, accessing skb->data + key_off is safe. So that's not a vulnerability.

Therefore, the main vulnerability is the race condition in the error counters. Also, the code may not validate that the ICMPv6 packet is a genuine error message for the tunnel. For example, an attacker could send a spoofed ICMPv6 packet with the right source/destination addresses to trigger MTU changes or log messages. However, this is a common issue with ICMP handling and not specific to this code. The code does perform a tunnel lookup, which requires that the tunnel exists, so it's mitigated to some extent.

So the final answer should flag the race condition in the error counters as a vulnerability. Also, maybe the MTU update without checking if the new MTU is reasonable beyond the minimum. But the code does set a minimum, so that's okay.

Another possible issue: the code uses t->dev->mtu = mtu; but if the tunnel device's MTU is changed, this could affect all traffic through that tunnel. However, this is the intended behavior when receiving a Packet Too Big message, as per Path MTU Discovery. So it's correct, but the code should ensure that the MTU is set appropriately. Since it's clamped to at least IPV6_MIN_MTU, it's safe.

So the main vulnerability is the race condition in the error counters. Therefore, the JSON should indicate that a vulnerability was detected, with the race condition as the issue.

commit_message:
Fixed frame allocation from an awaited frame.

njs_function_frame_save() is used to save the awaited frame when "await"
instruction is encountered. The saving was done as a memcpy() of
existing runtime frame.

njs_function_frame_alloc() is used to alloc a new function frame, this
function tries to use a spare preallocated memory from the previous
frame first.  Previously, this function might result in "use-after-free"
when invoked from a restored frame saved with njs_function_frame_save().
Because njs_function_frame_save() left pointers to the spare memory of
the original frame which may be already free when saved frame is
restored.

The fix is to erase fields for the spare memory from the saved frame.

This closes #469 issue on Github.

The 'dir' parameter in xfrm_migrate() is a user-controlled byte which is used
as an array index. This can lead to an out-of-bound access, kernel lockup and
DoS. Add a check for the 'dir' value.

This fixes CVE-2017-11600.

References: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1474928

commit_message:
Bluetooth: virtio_bt: fix memory leak in virtbt_rx_handle()

On the reception of packets with an invalid packet type, the memory of
the allocated socket buffers is never freed. Add a default case that frees
these to avoid a memory leak.

Fixes: afd2daa26c7a ("Bluetooth: Add support for virtio transport driver")
Signed-off-by: Soenke Huster <soenke.huster@eknoes.de>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
cve_desc: drivers/bluetooth/virtio_bt.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.3 has a memory leak (socket buffers have memory allocated but not freed).
reasoning:
<think>
Okay, let's tackle this. The user wants me to act as a Security Analyst and determine if the provided code has vulnerabilities. The code is a function called virtbt_rx_handle which processes Bluetooth packets in a Linux kernel context, I think. The function takes a struct virtio_bluetooth and a struct sk_buff. 

First, I'll look at the code step by step. The function starts by declaring a __u8 variable pkt_type. Then it assigns pkt_type by dereferencing the first byte of skb->data. Then it calls skb_pull(skb, 1), which removes the first byte from the skb. Then there's a switch statement checking pkt_type against several HCI packet types. If it matches, it sets hci_skb_pkt_type and calls hci_recv_frame. Otherwise, it frees the skb.

The main thing here is the initial access to skb->data. The code doesn't check if the skb is valid or if it has at least one byte. In kernel development, sk_buffs can sometimes be empty or have zero length. If skb->data is NULL or the length is zero, accessing the first byte would cause a null pointer dereference or access invalid memory. That's a classic vulnerability leading to a crash or potential information leak.

The author's explanation mentions that the code assumes the skb has data, which is a problem. The code should check that skb->len is at least 1 before accessing skb->data. Without that check, any empty or malformed packet could trigger this issue. 

Another point is the default case freeing the skb. That's okay if the protocol only expects those packet types, but if there are other valid types, they'd be dropped. However, the question is about vulnerabilities, not protocol correctness. The main issue here is the lack of input validation on the skb's data length.

So, the vulnerability detected is a potential null pointer dereference due to missing validation of skb->data. The confidence is high because in kernel code, such checks are crucial. The reasoning is that without checking the skb's length, the code could access invalid memory, leading to a crash or information disclosure.

commit_message:
Fix crash in MatrixSolve when inputs have different batch dimensions.

Before, the process would crash or certain elements would be silently ignored. Now an InvalidArgument is raised.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 384844020
Change-Id: Iba44417e383bdd0e1abc4012bfca83b2377dd335
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions several TensorFlow operations are missing validation for the shapes of the tensor arguments involved in the call. Depending on the API, this can result in undefined behavior and segfault or `CHECK`-fail related crashes but in some scenarios writes and reads from heap populated arrays are also possible. We have discovered these issues internally via tooling while working on improving/testing GPU op determinism. As such, we don't have reproducers and there will be multiple fixes for these issues. These fixes will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
ipf: release unhandled packets from the batch

Since 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, ...") the ipf
framework unconditionally allocates a new dp_packet to track
individual fragments.  This prevents a use-after-free.  However, an
additional issue was present - even when the packet buffer is cloned,
if the ip fragment handling code keeps it, the original buffer is
leaked during the refill loop.  Even in the original processing code,
the hardcoded dnsteal branches would always leak a packet buffer from
the refill loop.

This can be confirmed with valgrind:

==717566== 16,672 (4,480 direct, 12,192 indirect) bytes in 8 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 390 of 390
==717566==    at 0x484086F: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:380)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc__ (util.c:137)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc (util.c:172)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new (dp-packet.c:153)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new_with_headroom (dp-packet.c:163)
==717566==    by 0x550AA6: netdev_linux_batch_rxq_recv_sock.constprop.0 (netdev-linux.c:1262)
==717566==    by 0x5512AF: netdev_linux_rxq_recv (netdev-linux.c:1511)
==717566==    by 0x4AB7E0: netdev_rxq_recv (netdev.c:727)
==717566==    by 0x47F00D: dp_netdev_process_rxq_port (dpif-netdev.c:4699)
==717566==    by 0x47FD13: dpif_netdev_run (dpif-netdev.c:5957)
==717566==    by 0x4331D2: type_run (ofproto-dpif.c:370)
==717566==    by 0x41DFD8: ofproto_type_run (ofproto.c:1768)
==717566==    by 0x40A7FB: bridge_run__ (bridge.c:3245)
==717566==    by 0x411269: bridge_run (bridge.c:3310)
==717566==    by 0x406E6C: main (ovs-vswitchd.c:127)

The fix is to delete the original packet when it isn't able to be
reinserted into the packet batch.  Subsequent valgrind runs show that
the packets are not leaked from the batch any longer.

Fixes: 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, and remove the 'do_not_steal' flag.")
Fixes: 4ea96698f667 ("Userspace datapath: Add fragmentation handling.")
Reported-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>

Signed-off-by: Aaron Conole <aconole@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: David Marchand <david.marchand@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>
Signed-off-by: Alin-Gabriel Serdean <aserdean@ovn.org>

commit_message:
Prevent memory leak in decoding PNG images.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409300653
Change-Id: I6182124c545989cef80cefd439b659095920763b
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. When decoding PNG images TensorFlow can produce a memory leak if the image is invalid. After calling `png::CommonInitDecode(..., &decode)`, the `decode` value contains allocated buffers which can only be freed by calling `png::CommonFreeDecode(&decode)`. However, several error case in the function implementation invoke the `OP_REQUIRES` macro which immediately terminates the execution of the function, without allowing for the memory free to occur. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
CVE-2022-31214: fixing the fix, one more time

the previous commit "CVE-2022-31214: fixing the fix"
made private-etc=fonts,fonts and similar commands
fail with an error

fix that regression by tolerating already existing
directories
cve_desc: A Privilege Context Switching issue was discovered in join.c in Firejail 0.9.68. By crafting a bogus Firejail container that is accepted by the Firejail setuid-root program as a join target, a local attacker can enter an environment in which the Linux user namespace is still the initial user namespace, the NO_NEW_PRIVS prctl is not activated, and the entered mount namespace is under the attacker's control. In this way, the filesystem layout can be adjusted to gain root privileges through execution of available setuid-root binaries such as su or sudo.

commit_message:
Fix overflow CHECK issue with `tf.raw_ops.UnsortedSegmentJoin`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370766155
Change-Id: I33e7c6626224e1060a8a4ab51ad5d861c6d4c63e
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a denial of service by controlling the values of `num_segments` tensor argument for `UnsortedSegmentJoin`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/a2a607db15c7cd01d754d37e5448d72a13491bdb/tensorflow/core/kernels/unsorted_segment_join_op.cc#L92-L93) assumes that the `num_segments` tensor is a valid scalar. Since the tensor is empty the `CHECK` involved in `.scalar<T>()()` that checks that the number of elements is exactly 1 will be invalidated and this would result in process termination. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
cve_desc: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

for a should be released.

cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can read from outside of bounds of heap allocated data by sending specially crafted illegal arguments to `tf.raw_ops.SdcaOptimizerV2`. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/sdca_internal.cc#L320-L353) does not check that the length of `example_labels` is the same as the number of examples. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit a4e138660270e7599793fa438cd7b2fc2ce215a6. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message:
fuse: fix live lock in fuse_iget()

Commit 5d069dbe8aaf ("fuse: fix bad inode") replaced make_bad_inode()
in fuse_iget() with a private implementation fuse_make_bad().

The private implementation fails to remove the bad inode from inode
cache, so the retry loop with iget5_locked() finds the same bad inode
and marks it bad forever.

kmsg snip:

[ ] rcu: INFO: rcu_sched self-detected stall on CPU
...
[ ]  ? bit_wait_io+0x50/0x50
[ ]  ? fuse_init_file_inode+0x70/0x70
[ ]  ? find_inode.isra.32+0x60/0xb0
[ ]  ? fuse_init_file_inode+0x70/0x70
[ ]  ilookup5_nowait+0x65/0x90
[ ]  ? fuse_init_file_inode+0x70/0x70
[ ]  ilookup5.part.36+0x2e/0x80
[ ]  ? fuse_init_file_inode+0x70/0x70
[ ]  ? fuse_inode_eq+0x20/0x20
[ ]  iget5_locked+0x21/0x80
[ ]  ? fuse_inode_eq+0x20/0x20
[ ]  fuse_iget+0x96/0x1b0

Fixes: 5d069dbe8aaf ("fuse: fix bad inode")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 5.10+
Signed-off-by: Amir Goldstein <amir73il@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
cve_desc: An issue was discovered in fs/fuse/fuse_i.h in the Linux kernel before 5.11.8. A "stall on CPU" can occur because a retry loop continually finds the same bad inode, aka CID-775c5033a0d1.

commit_message:
selinux,smack: fix subjective/objective credential use mixups

Jann Horn reported a problem with commit eb1231f73c4d ("selinux:
clarify task subjective and objective credentials") where some LSM
hooks were attempting to access the subjective credentials of a task
other than the current task.  Generally speaking, it is not safe to
access another task's subjective credentials and doing so can cause
a number of problems.

Further, while looking into the problem, I realized that Smack was
suffering from a similar problem brought about by a similar commit

commit_message:
PCI: rpadlpar: Fix potential drc_name corruption in store functions

Both add_slot_store() and remove_slot_store() try to fix up the
drc_name copied from the store buffer by placing a NUL terminator at
nbyte + 1 or in place of a '\n' if present. However, the static buffer
that we copy the drc_name data into is not zeroed and can contain
anything past the n-th byte.

This is problematic if a '\n' byte appears in that buffer after nbytes
and the string copied into the store buffer was not NUL terminated to
start with as the strchr() search for a '\n' byte will mark this
incorrectly as the end of the drc_name string resulting in a drc_name
string that contains garbage data after the n-th byte.

Additionally it will cause us to overwrite that '\n' byte on the stack
with NUL, potentially corrupting data on the stack.

The following debugging shows an example of the drmgr utility writing
"PHB 4543" to the add_slot sysfs attribute, but add_slot_store()
logging a corrupted string value.

  drmgr: drmgr: -c phb -a -s PHB 4543 -d 1
  add_slot_store: drc_name = PHB 4543°|<82>!, rc = -19

Fix this by using strscpy() instead of memcpy() to ensure the string
is NUL terminated when copied into the static drc_name buffer.
Further, since the string is now NUL terminated the code only needs to
change '\n' to '\0' when present.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Tyrel Datwyler <tyreld@linux.ibm.com>
[mpe: Reformat change log and add mention of possible stack corruption]
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>

This occurs because add_slot_store and remove_slot_store mishandle drc_name '\0' termination, aka CID-cc7a0bb058b8.

commit_message:
Prevent copying uninitialized data in `AssignOp`.

This prevents harder to debug undefined behaviors that cannot be traced back to the original tensor after assignments occur earlier in the graph execution. Several of these undefined behaviors are just reference bindings to null pointers, which are caught when running under ubsan/asan.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408654780
Change-Id: Iad2ec40d43f5fd7ea016c20283356c12d5ddeab1
cve_desc: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `AssignOp` can result in copying uninitialized data to a new tensor. This later results in undefined behavior. The implementation has a check that the left hand side of the assignment is initialized (to minimize number of allocations), but does not check that the right hand side is also initialized. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_message: Fixed bug #68665 (Invalid free)
cve_desc: The apprentice_load function in libmagic/apprentice.c in the Fileinfo component in PHP through 5.6.4 attempts to perform a free operation on a stack-based character array, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption or application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via unknown vectors.  NOTE: this is disputed by the vendor because the standard erealloc behavior makes the free operation unreachable
reasoning:
<think>
Okay, let's tackle this. The user wants me to act as a Security Analyst and determine if the provided C code has any vulnerabilities. The instructions say to be cautious, flag even minor issues, and consider the absence of security measures as a vulnerability.

First, I'll read through the code carefully. The function apprentice_load handles loading magic entries from files or directories. It uses various memory management functions like ecalloc, erealloc, estrndup, and efree, which are common in PHP extensions. 

Looking at the code structure, there's a part where they handle directories. They use snprintf to build a path into mfn, which is a char array on the stack (char mfn[MAXPATHLEN]). Then, after checking the length, they use estrndup to copy the path into a dynamically allocated string stored in filearr. 

Wait, in the error handling block after realloc fails, there's a line: efree(mfn);. But mfn is a stack variable, not dynamically allocated. Using efree on it is incorrect and leads to undefined behavior. That's a definite vulnerability. The code should not free stack memory. This is a critical issue because it can cause crashes or memory corruption.

Another point is the use of MAXPATHLEN. If the directory path (fn) is very long, adding "/filename" might exceed MAXPATHLEN, leading to truncation. However, the code checks mflen after snprintf. If mflen is negative, it treats it as an error. But if the path is truncated, the resulting mfn might not be a valid path, leading to stat() failing later. However, the code checks stat(mfn, &st) == -1 and skips such files. So while truncation could happen, the code handles the error by skipping invalid entries. This might not be a direct vulnerability but could lead to denial of service if paths are too long, but the code seems to handle it.

The FIXME comment mentions sorting filenames to prevent non-determinism, which they address with qsort and cmpstrp. That's a design choice to ensure consistent processing, so that's handled.

In the error handling, when realloc fails for filearr, they efree(mfn), which is wrong. That's the main issue here. Also, in the same block, they call php_stream_closedir(dir) and goto out. But the efree(mfn) is incorrect.

Other parts of the code seem to handle memory correctly: when allocating filearr, they check for NULL and handle OOM. They also properly free allocated memory in the 'out' section when errors occur.

So the primary vulnerability is the incorrect use of efree on a stack variable. That's a clear bug. The JSON should reflect that. The confidence is high because it's a straightforward memory management error. The absence of proper error handling here is a vulnerability.
</think>

seq_file: disallow extremely large seq buffer allocations

int overflow pitfalls.

commit_message:
Prevent a division by 0 in division ops.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385223169
Change-Id: Ia4228960b5d2aa44480385f74bdd70d21a3613c3
cve_desc: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of division in TFLite is [vulnerable to a division by 0 error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/div.cc). There is no check that the divisor tensor does not contain zero elements. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 1e206baedf8bef0334cca3eb92bab134ef525a28. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.
reasoning:
<think>
Okay, let's take a look at this code. The function Eval is part of a TensorFlow Lite division operation. The code starts by getting parameters and op data using reinterpret_cast, which is common in TFLite but can be unsafe if the casts are incorrect. Then it retrieves input and output tensors.

The main logic checks the output tensor's type and calls different evaluation functions. For float32 or int32, it uses EvalDiv with a kernel_type. For uint8, it uses EvalQuantized. If the type isn't supported, it reports an error.

Now, the author's explanation mentions that the code assumes the input tensors are valid and have the correct types. But the code doesn't check the input tensor types. For example, when the output is UINT8, the code assumes the inputs are quantized, but there's no validation. If the inputs are not quantized or have incorrect parameters, this could lead to issues like incorrect results or crashes.

The problem here is that the code relies on the output type to decide the computation path but doesn't verify that the input tensors match the expected types for that path. This could lead to type confusion or memory corruption if the inputs are not properly set up. The absence of input type validation is a vulnerability because it assumes the inputs are correct without checking.

So, the vulnerability is that the code doesn't validate input tensor types against the output type. This could lead to using the wrong kernel functions with incompatible data types, causing undefined behavior. The fix would be to add checks for input tensor types before proceeding with the evaluation.
</think>

}

            Ex mode.
Solution:   Use "*" instead of "'<,'>" for Visual mode.

commit_message:
Ensure that bundles have metadata on install

If we have a bundle without metadata we wouldn't properly present
the permissions in the transaction.
cve_desc: Flatpak is a Linux application sandboxing and distribution framework. Prior to versions 1.12.3 and 1.10.6, Flatpak doesn't properly validate that the permissions displayed to the user for an app at install time match the actual permissions granted to the app at runtime, in the case that there's a null byte in the metadata file of an app. Therefore apps can grant themselves permissions without the consent of the user. Flatpak shows permissions to the user during install by reading them from the "xa.metadata" key in the commit metadata. This cannot contain a null terminator, because it is an untrusted GVariant. Flatpak compares these permissions to the *actual* metadata, from the "metadata" file to ensure it wasn't lied to. However, the actual metadata contents are loaded in several places where they are read as simple C-style strings. That means that, if the metadata file includes a null terminator, only the content of the file from *before* the terminator gets compared to xa.metadata. Thus, any permissions that appear in the metadata file after a null terminator are applied at runtime but not shown to the user. So maliciously crafted apps can give themselves hidden permissions. Users who have Flatpaks installed from untrusted sources are at risk in case the Flatpak has a maliciously crafted metadata file, either initially or in an update. This issue is patched in versions 1.12.3 and 1.10.6. As a workaround, users can manually check the permissions of installed apps by checking the metadata file or the xa.metadata key on the commit metadata.

commit_message:
Unsquashfs: fix write outside destination directory exploit

An issue on Github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
shows how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and ..) can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by checking all names for
validity.

In doing so I have also added checks for '.' and for names that
are shorter than they should be (names in the file system should
not have '\0' terminators).

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
cve_desc: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-1.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 stores the filename in the directory entry; this is then used by unsquashfs to create the new file during the unsquash. The filename is not validated for traversal outside of the destination directory, and thus allows writing to locations outside of the destination.

bgpd: Make sure hdr length is at a minimum of what is expected

Ensure that if the capability length specified is enough data.

Signed-off-by: Donald Sharp <sharpd@nvidia.com>
cve_desc: An out-of-bounds read in the BGP daemon of FRRouting FRR before 8.4 may lead to a segmentation fault and denial of service. This occurs in bgp_capability_msg_parse in bgpd/bgp_packet.c.
